content: I want to build an app to save and manage bookmarks.

I'm set up to work with you as a facilitator. Before building anything, I want to make sure I understand what you're really after — so we build the right thing. Let me start with the goal itself, not the features.

A few questions to get the direction right:

1. **When this is finished, what should be different from how things are for you now?** For example — are you losing track of links you meant to come back to? Scattered across browser tabs, chat messages, notes? Something else?

2. **Why bookmarks specifically?** Is saving-and-finding links the real heart of it, or is that a means to something bigger — like organizing research, keeping a reading list, sharing collections with others, or building a personal reference library?

3. **Is this mainly for you alone**, or will other people use it too?

You don't need to answer in any technical way at all — just tell me, in your own words, the situation you're trying to improve. Once I understand the goal, I'll show you working screens you can actually click through, and we'll shape it together from there.

I’m constantly leaving useful links in open tabs, messages to myself, and random notes, then I can’t find them when I need them. I want one calm, readable place where I can save a link quickly, find it again by searching or organizing it with tags, and keep track of things I still mean to read.

The bigger goal is a dependable personal reference library. I’d like saved links to retain useful page details automatically, and ideally preserve the content in case the original page later changes or disappears. I also want to be able to put older links away without permanently deleting them.

This is mainly for me alone. Sharing and collaboration aren’t important for the first version.

content:
That's a clear and vivid picture — thank you. Let me play back what I understood, so we're sure we're aimed at the same thing:

**The goal:** Today, useful links slip away — stranded in open tabs, self-messages, and scattered notes — and you can't find them when you need them. You want *one calm, readable place* where you can:

- **Save a link quickly**, without friction
- **Find it again** later, by searching or by organizing with tags
- **Keep track of what you still mean to read**
- **Tuck older links away** when you're done with them, without permanently deleting them

And the deeper purpose is a **dependable personal reference library** — one you can trust over time. Two things serve that trust: saved links should **automatically keep useful details about the page** (so an entry is recognizable, not just a bare URL), and ideally the app would **preserve a copy of the page's content** so it survives even if the original later changes or vanishes.

It's **for you alone** for now — sharing can wait.

Two quick things before we start shaping actual screens:

1. **Is that direction right, and did I miss anything?**

2. You mentioned preserving a copy of page content as *"ideally"* — I want to make sure I prioritize correctly. **If the very first working version had to launch with only some of this, which parts are essential to you, and which could come a little later?** (No wrong answer — this just tells me where to start.)

And so I prototype it in the right shape: **where do you picture using this most — in a web browser on your computer, on your phone, as a desktop app, or somewhere else?**

Yes, that direction is right. The essential first version is quick saving, automatically filling in recognizable page details, a readable list, strong search, tags, and a clear way to separate unread, finished, and archived links. I also need to be able to correct or add details and notes after saving. If I accidentally save the same address again, I’d expect to be taken to the existing entry instead of ending up with duplicates.

Preserving a local copy of the page is important to the long-term goal, but it can come after that basic experience is solid. Importing my existing browser bookmarks would also be useful later.

I picture using it mainly in a web browser on my computer. It should still be comfortable on a phone for quickly saving or looking up a link, but I don’t need a separate mobile app.

Clean slate confirmed — the port is free with no stale processes, so the new build (iteration 2) will load when you open it. It starts with **five sample entries I preloaded** so you can try the reading-status behaviour immediately, without having to save a bunch of links first.

Here's what's new to explore: your links are now separated into **three groups — To read, Finished, and Archived** — shown as tabs at the top, and each entry carries a small **status badge** so you always see where it stands (that's the "status visible on each entry" you asked for). New saves land in **To read**. **Archived** items are tucked out of To-read and Finished but *not deleted* — they stay in the Archived group and can be brought back.

Because there are a few natural ways to actually *change* an entry's status, I built **three interaction styles that are identical except for that one thing**, so you can feel the difference and pick. There's a switcher at the bottom of the page, and here are direct links:

- **Style A — [http://maker:4001/?ui=a](http://maker:4001/?ui=a)**: each entry shows its status as a small pill; click it to pick a different group from a little menu.
- **Style B — [http://maker:4001/?ui=b](http://maker:4001/?ui=b)**: each entry has clear labelled buttons — *Mark finished*, *Archive*, *Restore*.
- **Style C — [http://maker:4001/?ui=c](http://maker:4001/?ui=c)**: a round checkbox to tick something as finished, plus a small archive icon.

**Please try this same action in each style:** take one of the *To read* items and mark it **Finished**, then **Archive** a different one — and watch them move between the tabs. Flip between the three styles using the links above.

Two things I'd like your judgment on:

1. **Do these three groups — To read, Finished, Archived — match how you actually think about your reading?** (Right names? Right number of groups?)
2. **Which of the three styles feels most natural** for changing an item's status — and does archiving feel like *putting away safely*, not deleting?

Style B feels most natural. The labelled actions make “Mark read,” “Archive,” and “Restore” immediately understandable; the checkbox and icon in Style C are a little too easy to misread, and Style A makes archiving look like a reading status.

I’d change the grouping before approving it, though. “Finished” and “Archived” shouldn’t be equivalent, mutually exclusive stages. A saved link can be read or unread, while archiving is a separate choice about whether it remains in my active library.

I’d prefer:

- **All**: every non-archived link, whether read or unread
- **Unread**: only links I still mean to read
- **Archived**: links I’ve put away

New saves should begin as unread. Marking one read should remove it from Unread but leave it in All. Archiving should remove it from both active views, and restoring it should preserve whether it was read or unread before. “Read” also feels more accurate than “Finished” for reference material.

That completes edge exploration across every feature block. Here's the **full settled scope** for your first version — in plain terms, everything you've approved:

**Saving & entries**
1. **Quick save with a review step** — paste a link; its details fill in automatically; you get a brief chance to correct the title/description (and add a note) before it's added, or discard.
2. **Recognizable entries** — each shows title, a short description, the site, its icon, and when you saved it.
3. **No duplicates** — re-saving an address (ignoring `http/https`, `www.`, trailing slash) takes you to the existing entry instead of copying it.

**Reading & keeping**
4. **Reading vs. archiving are independent** — Unread/Read is separate from active/archived, across three views: **All / Unread / Archived**. Archiving *puts away* without deleting; restoring keeps the prior read state.

**Organizing & finding**
5. **Tags** on every entry — add/remove with suggestions; filter by one or several at once (match all), within the current view.
6. **Editing** — fix the title, description, or the **address itself** (with the same duplicate guard), and add a **formatted personal note** (headings, bold, lists, links) shown distinctly from the page's own description.
7. **Strong search** within the current view — all-words matching, `"exact phrases"`, `#tag`, `AND/OR/NOT`, parentheses, highlighted results, and a **Search tips** link.
8. **Sort** — newest added / oldest added / title.

**Holding up at scale & edges**
9. **Large library** — Load more in ~25 batches, while search, filters, and counts always cover everything.
10. **Long content** — two-line titles, clamped descriptions, and a note preview with *Show full note*.
11. **Times** — relative when recent, actual dates (with year when needed) after about a week.
12. **Empty states & save errors** — calm empty messages; a clear message for a bad address; an unreachable page still saveable with details you type in.

It's a **web app for your computer, comfortable on a phone** — for you alone.

**Recorded for later (not in this build):** preserving a local copy of each page's content; importing existing browser bookmarks; and an optional "fetch details from a new address" action when you change an address. Sharing stays out of scope.

---

That's **13 settled feature flows.** May I now start building this scope for real — the actual application, not the exploratory prototype?

Not quite yet. The summary captures what we approved, but a few important first-version behaviors are missing:

- I need a clearly separate **Delete permanently** action. Archive must remain reversible; deletion should require confirmation and remove the link for good.
- For a large library, I need to select several links—or every link matching the current view, search, and tag filters—and then add/remove tags, mark read/unread, archive, or delete them together.
- Clicking an entry’s title should open the original page.
- Along with the title, description, and icon, saving should collect the page’s preview image when one is available, even if the calm list doesn’t always display it.

Please add those to the settled first-version scope. With those included, you may begin building the real application.

---

## Your bookmark library is built and ready

**Open it: [http://maker:4000](http://maker:4000)** — it starts as an empty library (a fresh, real app, not the prototype). Everything you save is stored and **persists across restarts**, so it's the dependable reference library you described.

**What it does — the behaviour you approved, all 17 flows:**
- **Save quickly** — paste a link, review the auto-filled title/description (and the page's preview image), then add it. No duplicates; re-saving an address takes you to the existing entry.
- **Read & keep** — Unread/Read and archiving are independent, across **All / Unread / Archived**. Archiving puts away without deleting; restoring keeps your reading state.
- **Organize** — tags on every entry, filter by one or several at once.
- **Edit** — fix the title, description, or the address itself, and write a **formatted note**; the preview image shows here and in the review, not in the calm list.
- **Find** — strong search within the current view: all-words, `"phrases"`, `#tag`, `AND/OR/NOT`, parentheses, highlighted, with a **Search tips** link. Sort by newest/oldest/title.
- **At scale** — Load more in batches, while counts and search cover everything; two-line titles; long-note previews; dates after about a week.
- **Manage in bulk** — multi-select (including **select all matching**) to tag, mark read/unread, archive, or delete together; selection clears when you change view/search/tags.
- **Delete permanently** — a separate, confirmed action, distinct from archive.
- Clicking a **title** opens the original page.

- **24 internal unit tests** (URL/duplicate identity, the search parser, time/formatting, and the full data layer including persistence) — all green.
